The business reported $522.09m revenue and a $24.84m net loss for the twelve months to March 31, 2026, with proceeds earmarked to repay debt.
why_it_matters: This is a partial monetisation, not an exit: Greenbriar keeps roughly 81% and control, so the IPO functions primarily as a deleveraging and price-discovery event ahead of staged secondary sell-downs. Applied Aerospace is a vertically integrated manufacturer of mission-critical hardware for space/launch, defence aviation and C5ISR/precision strike, so the revenue is programme-driven and backlog-backed rather than infrastructure-contracted, with margin currently suppressed by a net loss on $522m of revenue. Taking a 2022-vintage buyout public at roughly $3.3bn implied value in under four years is a strong marker for Greenbriar's Fund VI and useful supporting evidence for the $5.4bn Fund VII it closed in February 2026. Watch the lock-up expiry and follow-on cadence, and whether defence budget momentum converts the backlog into positive net income.

headline: 23 states have now approved large-load tariffs, with Virginia requiring 14-year minimum contracts and $1.5M/MW collateral
players: A Columbia Climate Law Blog analysis published June 2, 2026 found that as of May 2026, 23 states had approved at least one large-load tariff and seven more had tariffs pending, with Ohio and Virginia adopting theirs in 2025 and Minnesota enacting HF 16 in June 2025. Typical protections include minimum contract terms of 14 years in Virginia and 12 years in Ohio, take-or-pay provisions requiring payment for contracted capacity regardless of use, exit fees, collateral of $1.5 million per MW in Virginia, and long-term fixed pricing. Clean transition tariffs, a related structure, allocate new-resource procurement across the data center developer, utility and an independent generator.
why_it_matters: Take-or-pay tariffs with 12-14 year terms convert data center load into something close to a contracted utility revenue stream, which is exactly what makes regulated grid capex and adjacent generation financeable at investment-grade cost of capital. For digital infrastructure sponsors it is the opposite: it lengthens fixed obligations, raises collateral posting, and makes speculative land-banking of powered shells materially more expensive. Expect the spread between sites with executed large-load tariff agreements and merely 'permitted' sites to widen sharply in M&A pricing. Watch the seven pending states and whether the collateral standard converges toward Virginia's $1.5m/MW.

headline: Goldman Sachs Alternatives raises over $3bn at first close for fourth-generation mid-market infrastructure fund
players: Goldman Sachs Alternatives announced on June 1, 2026 an aggregated first close of over $3 billion for West Street Infrastructure Partners V against a $4 billion target, reaching 75% of target. The fund targets mid-market infrastructure operating businesses across four themes: energy transition, digital infrastructure, transportation and logistics, and circular economy. Eighty percent of initial commitments came from investors in prior vintages. The fund has already closed one investment, QScale, a Canadian data centre platform, on May 13, 2026.
why_it_matters: Hitting 75% of target at first close with 80% re-ups is a strong fundraising signal in a market where many infrastructure managers have extended timelines, and it confirms LP capital is still flowing to mid-market operating-business strategies rather than core yield. The inclusion of transportation and logistics alongside digital and energy transition means more dry powder chasing logistics platforms, terminals and transport services businesses in the sub-$500m enterprise value range — expect entry multiples in that band to stay firm. That the first deal is a data centre rather than a transport asset is a reminder of where capital is actually being deployed within these mandates. Watch the final close size and the pace of transport deployment.

headline: US public pension commitments to infrastructure funds fell to $17.4B across 165 commitments in 2025, down from $21.3B
players: The Reason Foundation's Annual Transportation Finance Report, covered by Bond Buyer on June 1, 2026, found US public pension commitments to infrastructure funds fell to 165 commitments totalling $17.4 billion in 2025, from 254 commitments totalling $21.3 billion in 2024 and 238 totalling $23.8 billion in 2023. Twenty-six states committed $13.3 billion, led by CalPERS at $1.8 billion, New Mexico at $1.4 billion, Washington at $1.3 billion and Connecticut at $1.2 billion. Report author Robert Poole said he was surprised by the decline and could not identify the driver.
why_it_matters: This is a hard data point cutting against the AI-infrastructure fundraising narrative: the largest single US LP cohort wrote 35% fewer cheques by count and 18% less by value year on year. It implies the mega-closes being announced are concentrating capital in a handful of brand-name managers while mid-market and first-time infrastructure funds face a genuinely tighter market. Expect continued barbelling — GPs with $10bn+ franchises and separate-account capability will keep raising, while everyone else extends timelines or accepts smaller final closes. Watch whether 2026 commitment counts recover and whether the gap is being filled by insurance, wealth and sovereign capital rather than US public plans.

headline: LBNL 'Queued Up' 2026: gas in interconnection queues jumps 86% to 253 GW as solar and storage volumes fall
players: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's Queued Up 2026 edition, published in June 2026 with data through end-2025, counts roughly 8,200 projects actively seeking interconnection representing 1,312 GW of generation and about 749 GW of storage. Natural gas capacity in the queues rose 86% to 253 GW while solar fell 19% to 773 GW, storage fell 16% to 749 GW and wind fell 19% to 220 GW; total active queue volume dropped about 10% year over year on high withdrawals. Only 13% of capacity that entered queues between 2000 and 2020 had reached commercial operation by end-2025, with 75% withdrawn; median time from interconnection request to COD exceeded five years for projects built in 2025. Some 549 GW has a draft or executed interconnection agreement but is not yet operating.
why_it_matters: An 86% jump in queued gas alongside falling renewables volumes is the clearest structural evidence that developer capital has rotated toward dispatchable capacity, and it front-runs the turbine and EPC bottleneck. The 13% historical completion rate and 549 GW sitting with signed interconnection agreements but no operation are the two numbers to apply as haircuts when valuing pipelines — a signed IA is necessary but far from sufficient. A five-year-plus median IR-to-COD also means anything not already in an advanced queue position cannot serve load before 2031. Watch whether the gas surge converts or withdraws once turbine delivery dates and tariff terms become firm.
